brief.situation: You are the security architect leading the technical response at Ostrander Group, a fictional manufacturer. At 10:00 the cloud identity team escalates: three administrator accounts signed in to the tenant with valid federation tokens and an MFA claim, from an address none of them use. You own the identity architecture. Decide how to restore trust, keep evidence and report.
handover: The on-premises federation servers (fs.example.com) issue sign-in tokens for the cloud tenant (mail, files, HR). Cloud-only break-glass administrator accounts exist and are tested.
Rotating the signing certificate makes every relying party re-read the federation metadata; expect sign-in errors while they do.
howItWorks: Each task takes analyst time: choose it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes that task takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you declare the incident contained, you notify, write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: how you knew the tokens were forged, the order you restored trust in and why, and what you changed in the architecture.

parts.label: Detection
parts.criteria: Identifies tokens with valid signatures and MFA claims but no issuance on the federation servers as forged with a stolen signing key (MFA does not help); traces the key theft to the service account.
parts.modelAnswer: The tokens validated and carried MFA claims, but the federation servers never issued them, so someone had the signing key. The certificate store log showed svc-fed-sync exporting it.

parts.label: Order of containment
parts.criteria: Removes the attacker's foothold on the identity tier before rotating (or cuts the federation trust); rotates twice so the stolen key is no longer trusted; then revokes sessions; then hunts for persistence made with forged access (app registrations, consents, credentials).
parts.modelAnswer: I disabled svc-fed-sync first, otherwise it would read the new key too; rotated the certificate twice; revoked every session; then listed new apps and consents and removed what the forged sessions made.

parts.label: Architecture
parts.criteria: Keeps images before rebuilding; moves the federation servers into a tier-0 enclave reachable only from privileged workstations, removes service accounts with key access, or moves to cloud-managed sign-in.
parts.modelAnswer: After imaging, the federation servers were rebuilt in the tier-0 enclave with no service account able to read the key; cloud-managed sign-in is the fallback if that cannot be held.

expertPath.text: Stand up incident command; review the federation servers' certificate access: svc-fed-sync took the key. Disable it.
Rotate the signing certificate twice and push the metadata; revoke every session.
Correlate sign-ins to confirm the forgery's extent; list new apps and consents; image the federation servers.
Rebuild the federation servers from clean media in the tier-0 enclave.
Notify the CISO, executives, legal and privacy, and relying-party owners; record the stolen key and the tier-0 change.

contained.headline: Good: trust rebuilt from the root
contained.body: MFA could not help against a stolen signing key. You closed the foothold that stole it, then replaced the key, then the sessions, then looked for what was left.

containedLate.headline: Contained, with gaps
containedLate.body: The attacker is out. The criteria show what cost you: a backdoor app, a second stolen key, or time.

breach.headline: Executive mail exported
breach.body: A single rotation leaves the old certificate trusted, and a session revoke while the key still works only makes the attacker mint new tokens.

evidenceLost.headline: Evidence wiped
evidenceLost.body: Image the identity tier before rebuilding it; it is the only record of how the key was taken.

stillIn.headline: Closed too soon
stillIn.body: Rotating while the attacker still controls a service account on the federation servers just hands them the new key; and access they already used can leave an app behind.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Valid, MFA-stamped tokens that the federation servers never issued mean the signing key is stolen. Find how (svc-fed-sync exported it), disable that account first, rotate the certificate twice in rapid succession (or cut the federation trust and use cloud-only break-glass accounts), revoke every session, then hunt for persistence made with forged access such as app registrations and consents. Image the federation servers before rebuilding them in a tier-0 enclave, and notify the CISO, executives, legal and privacy, and every relying-party owner.
